articles.body: O fornecedor de IA jurídica não tem o mesmo interesse que você em revisar o que ela decide O padrão que se repete entre um plugin de loja e uma ferramenta jurídica Em abril um cliente me mandou, lado a lado com a minha proposta, a de um concorrente. Queria saber se eu conhecia os plugins que esse outro profissional recomendava no lugar dos meus. Segundo ele, eram "100% confiáveis e gratuitos", porque o criador ganhava por fora, pela venda que o plugin empurrava. Respondi que sim, conhecia o modelo, e expliquei por que tanta gente cria peça de loja sem a mínima segurança assim: o fornecedor lucra com o volume que o plugin gera, não com a qualidade dele. Ninguém tinha mentido sobre o preço. A mentira estava em "100% confiável".

articles.title: Before you rent the GPUs, check the map: I built a CLI that picks your LLM serving engine
articles.excerpt: DeepInfer collected ~19k stars in a single week (GitHub Trending scan 2026-10-28). The headlines say "production inference engine". My weekend said: it serves exactly one model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash),…
articles.body: DeepInfer collected ~19k stars in a single week (GitHub Trending scan 2026-10-28). The headlines say "production inference engine". My weekend said: it serves exactly one model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), needs SM100+ or Ascend950 silicon, and runs offline-only with no KV cache system, no PD disaggregation, no load balancing. Checked against the upstream repo 2026-11-01. That is not a knock. That is the gap a tool should close: before you rent GPUs or rewire your stack, you need the map — what you actually have, what the model actually costs in memory, and which engines are actually viable on that combination. So I built servefit : a zero-dependency Python CLI that inventories your hardware, does the memory math, checks a dated engine-support matrix, and recommends an engine with reasons.
articles.author: TECHDEV

articles.title: Multi-campus inside a multi-tenant Laravel app: our reads were airtight, our writes were not
articles.excerpt: We build Karobar, a school management system for schools in Pakistan. It is a Laravel API with a database per school (tenant), and a React front end. Then schools started asking for a second campus. T…
articles.body: We build Karobar , a school management system for schools in Pakistan. It is a Laravel API with a database per school (tenant), and a React front end. Then schools started asking for a second campus. This post covers how we added campuses inside a tenant, and five rules we learned the hard way. The biggest lesson: we tested who could read a campus's rows, and never tested where a write could land. Tenant vs campus: why a campus is not a tenant The obvious move is "one campus = one tenant". We didn't do that. A school with three campuses is still one school: one curriculum, one fee structure, one owner who wants a single number for "fees collected this month". Separate databases would turn every school-wide question into a cross-database job.
articles.author: Naveed Malik

articles.title: The Ghost in the Machine: Engineering AI Tribute Apps for Abandoned Software
articles.excerpt: Originally published on tamiz.pro. Software is immortal until it isn't. One day Google Reader is the backbone of your morning routine; the next, a shutdown notice, a 503, and then — silence. The code…
articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . Software is immortal until it isn't. One day Google Reader is the backbone of your morning routine; the next, a shutdown notice, a 503, and then — silence. The code doesn't vanish, though. It lives on in forks, in tarballs on dead FTP servers, in Wayback Machine snapshots, in the commit history of a repository nobody has pushed to in a decade. A tribute app is a new class of application built on top of that digital sediment: an AI-powered system that resurrects abandoned software not as a static archive, but as an interactive presence. You can ask it questions, watch it "think," and even pair-program with its ghost.
articles.author: Tamiz Uddin

articles.title: I built an AI reply tool. The hard part was deciding what it could see and do.
articles.excerpt: I build Riffwise, a Chrome extension that drafts replies from the conversation already open. This is a product-building note, not a benchmark: the question I keep coming back to is not “Can AI write a…
articles.body: I build Riffwise, a Chrome extension that drafts replies from the conversation already open. This is a product-building note, not a benchmark: the question I keep coming back to is not “Can AI write a sentence?” It is “What should an AI writing tool be allowed to see and do?” A reply assistant sits close to somebody else’s words. That makes its trust boundary part of the product, not a footnote. 1. Make the request explicit The user starts a reply or quote-draft action. Riffwise reads the relevant post or email context for that request. The writing request is sent to OpenAI to generate the draft. That is a cloud AI call, and users should be able to understand that before they use it.

articles.title: HackerTube vs. YouTube Recommendations: Curated Signal or Personal Fit?
articles.excerpt: A video can be excellent and still never appear on your screen. That is the problem HackerTube tries to solve, but not by making a better version of YouTube's recommendation model. It changes the sour…
articles.body: A video can be excellent and still never appear on your screen. That is the problem HackerTube tries to solve, but not by making a better version of YouTube's recommendation model. It changes the source of the recommendations. HackerTube starts with videos that people recommended in Hacker News comments over almost two decades. YouTube's homepage, by contrast, is personalized around your own viewing history and other signals. One system asks, in effect, "What has this community found worth sharing?" The other asks, "What might this particular viewer want next?" That difference makes HackerTube an unusually clear comparison of two discovery strategies: a shared human-curated corpus versus an individualized platform feed. Neither is automatically better.

articles.title: This Android gaming benchmark app does something I’ve never seen before
articles.excerpt: Evolve is a new gaming benchmark that shows you where mobile GPUs are hitting a bottleneck.
articles.body: Credit: Harish Jonnalagadda / Android Authority I like benchmarks a little too much and use them on every new phone I test. Synthetic benchmarks like Geekbench and 3DMark do a good job of simulating real-world usage and gaming scenarios, and they predict a device’s performance potential reasonably well. As someone who gets over 75 phones a year, a synthetic benchmark lets me easily measure how a particular device holds up against its predecessor. There’s a new benchmark that aims to go beyond just delivering an overall score. It’s called Evolve , and it provides useful insights across five metrics, allowing you to then pinpoint which part of the GPU is handling modern workloads well, and what’s causing a potential bottleneck.

articles.title: 5 bright planets to spot in November — when and where to see them
articles.excerpt: From a close encounter between Mars and Jupiter to dazzling Venus and elusive Mercury, November offers plenty of planetary highlights. Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: This is a great month for planet watching, either in the evenings or mornings. During convenient evening hours, the planet of choice is Saturn , visible well up in the southern sky during mid-to-late evening hours. Telescopically, the southern side of its famous ring system is currently tilted about 6½ degrees to our line of sight. Around the middle of the night, Mars and Jupiter come into view above the east-northeast horizon and just before the break of dawn are in excellent position, soaring high in the southern sky in the vicinity of the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Watch how Mars approaches Jupiter early in the month, passes it on Nov. 16, then spends the rest of the month sailing away to the east.

articles.excerpt: Jack Nicholson delivered mob cinema's ultimate statement of power.
articles.body: In crime cinema, a lethal line of dialogue can carry just as much weight as a loaded gun. Martin Scorsese's Goodfellas hooks audiences with Henry Hill's seductive declaration, “As far back as I can remember, I always wanted to be a gangster,” framing a life of crime as the ultimate aspiration. Miller's Crossing features Tom Reagan's wonderfully blunt take on underworld survival, while Casino , Scarface , and The Godfather overflow with dialogue that has long since bled into the cultural lexicon. Immortal phrases like “keep your friends close, but your enemies closer” and “an offer you can’t refuse” remain cinematic icons right alongside the actors and directors who brought them to life.

articles.body: Somewhere in Middle-earth, is there a Chili’s that serves orcs? Does an Uruk-hai host greet hungry customers, tell them it’ll be a 20-minute wait, and hand them a menu? Does the kitchen run out of manflesh halfway through the dinner rush? Is halfling served as an appetizer? What precisely is in the Triple Dipper? These are unreasonable questions to ask of an otherwise perfect fantasy epic. Unfortunately, The Lord of the Rings : The Two Towers invites every one of them with one line that feels deeply anachronistic.

articles.title: 9 nightmarish sci-fi spaceships to crawl aboard for Halloween if you dare
articles.excerpt: Grab your high-lumen flashlight and gargantuan gun to explore these vicious vessels
articles.body: Abandoned, possessed, or infested spaceships in sci-fi films, books, and video games are usually not a welcoming place to hang your helmet and kick back inside. Many are distinctly marked as DO NOT APPROACH zones and equipped with clearly articulated warning messages to keep your distance, but that doesn't ever seem to stop scavengers, space pirates, or evil industrial mega corporations from waving off these dangerous signs to board anyway. Other creaky craft are apt to contain nasty alien hitchhikers or biological hazards not exactly conducive to a pleasant star-trekking voyage. Whether these nefarious neglected craft have just reappeared from the other side of a black hole or have been lying dormant for eons on a hostile planetoid, visitors are usually infrequent.

articles.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 234 — Living in Lunar Caves
articles.excerpt: On Episode 234 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Mike Wall are joined by Than Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute about a NASA-backed payload bound for the Marius Hills Pit on the moon.
articles.body: On Episode 234 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Mike Wall are joined by Than Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute about a NASA-backed payload bound for the Marius Hills Pit on the moon. In our ongoing quest to develop a moon base, could we possibly utilize the area beneath the surface of the moon in order to make the moon habitable? Could Marius Hills Pit, a roughly 50-meter-wide opening that may lead into a lunar lava tube, become the Moon's first living habitat for humans? Putzig explains how geophysical instruments on a rover could detect hidden voids beneath the surface and measure the size of these lava tubes.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
